## Genetics
[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/GEM_corn.jpg/250px-GEM_corn.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GEM_corn.jpg)
Exotic varieties are collected to add [genetic diversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_diversity "Genetic diversity") when [selectively breeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_breeding "Crop breeding") new domestic [strains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strain_(biology) "Strain (biology)").

## Genetics
Maize is [diploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploid "Diploid") with 20 [chromosomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosome "Chromosome"). 83% of [allelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele "Allele") variation within the genome derives from its teosinte ancestors, primarily due to the freedom of _Zea_ species to [outcross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outcross "Outcross").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Back-to-the-Wild-11)[Barbara McClintock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_McClintock "Barbara McClintock") used maize to validate her [transposon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposon "Transposon") theory of "jumping genes", for which she won the 1983 [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-12) Maize remains an important [model organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_organism "Model organism") for genetics and [developmental biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developmental_biology "Developmental biology").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Strable_Scanlon_2009-13) The [MADS-box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MADS-box "MADS-box") motif is involved in the development of maize flowers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Friedman-et-al-2004-14)

## Genetics
The Maize Genetics and Genomics Database is funded by the [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture") (USDA) to support maize research.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-15) The [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") maintains a large collection of maize accessions tested and cataloged for insect resistance.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Breeding-Towards-16) In 2005, the U.S. [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), the USDA, and the [Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") formed a consortium to sequence the maize [genome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome"). The resulting [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") sequence data was deposited immediately into [GenBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GenBank "GenBank"), a public repository for genome-sequence data.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-17) Sequencing of the maize genome was completed in 2008.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-18) In 2009, the consortium published results of its sequencing effort.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-19) The genome, 85% of which is composed of [transposons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposon "Transposon"), contains 32,540 genes. Much of it has been duplicated and reshuffled by [helitrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helitron_(biology) "Helitron (biology)"), a group of [transposable elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposable_element "Transposable element") within maize's DNA.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-20)

## Taxonomy
### External phylogeny
The maize [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus")_Zea_ is relatively closely related to [sorghum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorghum "Sorghum"), both being in the [PACMAD clade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PACMAD_clade "PACMAD clade") of Old World grasses, and much more distantly to [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") and [wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheat "Wheat"), which are in the other major group of grasses, the [BOP clade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOP_clade "BOP clade"). It is closely related to _[Tripsacum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripsacum "Tripsacum")_, gamagrass.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Gaut_Le_Thierry_dEnnequin_Peek_Sawkins_2000-21)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Cornselection.jpg/250px-Cornselection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cornselection.jpg)
Teosinte (left), maize-teosinte hybrid (middle), maize (right)
Maize is the [domesticated variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_domestication "Crop domestication") of the four species of [teosintes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte"), which are its [crop wild relatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) Teosinte was likely used by hunter-gatherers because it added security to their food supply, being that it was adaptable to changes in climate and environment.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Lohse_Morgan_Jones_2022-2) The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the Russian botanist [Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Ivanovich_Vavilov "Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov") in 1931, and the American [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize")-winner [George Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Beadle "George Beadle") in 1932.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23):10 The two plants have dissimilar appearance, maize having a single tall stalk with multiple leaves and teosinte being a short, bushy plant.

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
The difference between the two is largely controlled by differences in just two genes, called grassy tillers-1 (_gt1_, [A0A317YEZ1](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/A0A317YEZ1)) and teosinte branched-1 (_tb1_, [Q93WI2](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q93WI2)).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) In the late 1930s, [Paul Mangelsdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Mangelsdorf "Paul Mangelsdorf") suggested that domesticated maize was the result of a hybridization event between an unknown wild maize and a species of _[Tripsacum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripsacum "Tripsacum")_, a related genus; this has been refuted by modern [genetic testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_testing "Genetic testing").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
In 2004, [John Doebley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doebley "John Doebley") identified Balsas teosinte, _Zea mays_ subsp. _parviglumis_, native to the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley in Mexico's southwestern highlands, as the [crop wild relative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative") genetically most similar to modern maize.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Wu-et-al-2011-25) The middle part of the short Balsas River valley is the likely location of early domestication. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700 year old layer of deposits in a cave not far from [Iguala, Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguala,_Guerrero "Iguala, Guerrero").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) Doebley and colleagues showed in 2002 that maize had been domesticated only once, about 9,000 years ago, and then spread throughout the Americas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
Maize pollen dated to 7,300 years ago from [San Andres, Tabasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andr%C3%A9s_(Mesoamerican_site) "San Andrés (Mesoamerican site)") has been found on the Caribbean coast.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) A primitive corn was being grown in southern Mexico, Central America, and northern South America 7,000 years ago. Archaeological remains of early maize ears, found at [Guila Naquitz Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guila_Naquitz_Cave "Guila Naquitz Cave") in the [Oaxaca Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca_Valley "Oaxaca Valley"), are roughly 6,250 years old; the oldest ears from caves near [Tehuacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehuac%C3%A1n,_Puebla "Tehuacán, Puebla"), Puebla, are 5,450 years old.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28)

## Taxonomy
### Spreading to the north
Around 4,500 years ago, maize began to spread to the north. Maize was first cultivated at several sites in New Mexico and Arizona about 4,100 years ago.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) During the first millennium AD, maize cultivation spread more widely in the areas north. In particular, the large-scale adoption of maize agriculture and consumption in eastern North America took place about A.D. 900. Native Americans cleared large forest and grassland areas for the new crop.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-29) The rise in maize cultivation 500 to 1,000 years ago in what is now the [southeastern U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_U.S. "Southeastern U.S.") corresponded with a decline of freshwater [mussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussel "Mussel"), which are very sensitive to environmental changes.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-30)

## Taxonomy
### Names
The name _maize_ derives from the Spanish form _maíz_ of the [Taíno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%ADno_language "Taíno language")_mahis_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-31) The Swedish botanist [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") used the common name maize as the species epithet in _Zea mays_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranum-32) The name _maize_ is preferred in formal, scientific, and international usage as a [common name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_name "Common name") because it refers specifically to this one grain, unlike _corn_, which has a complex variety of meanings that vary by context and geographic region.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) Most countries primarily use the term _maize_, and the name _corn_ is used mainly in the U.S.

## Taxonomy
### Names
and a handful of other English-speaking countries.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OxfordEncyclopedia-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Espinoza_2015-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-36) In countries that primarily use the term _maize_, the word _corn_ may denote any [cereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal "Cereal") crop, varying geographically with the local [staple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OED_corn-37) such as wheat in England and oats in Scotland or Ireland.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) The usage of _corn_ for maize started as a shortening of "[Indian corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_corn "Flint corn")" in 18th-century North America.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mencken-38)
The historian of food [Betty Fussell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Fussell "Betty Fussell") writes in an article on the history of the word _corn_ in North America that "[t]o say the word _corn_ is to plunge into the tragi-farcical mistranslations of language and history".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39) Similar to the British usage, the Spanish referred to maize as _panizo_, a generic term for cereal grains, as did Italians with the term _polenta_. The British later referred to maize as Turkey wheat, Turkey corn, or Indian corn; Fussell comments that "they meant not a place but a condition, a savage rather than a civilized grain".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)

## Taxonomy
### Names
International groups such as the [Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Agriculture_and_Bioscience_International "Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International") consider _maize_ the preferred common name.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-40) The word _maize_ is used by the UN's [Food and Agriculture Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-41) and in the names of the [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") of Mexico, the Indian Institute of Maize Research,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-42) the Maize Association of Australia,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-43) the National Maize Association of Nigeria,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-44) the National Maize Association of Ghana,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-45) the Maize Trust of South Africa,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-46) and the Zimbabwe Seed Maize Association.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Rusike_Donovan_1995-47) In the United States, _maize_ can be used interchangeably with the term _corn_.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-48)

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg/250px-Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg)
Ancient Mesoamerican relief sculpture of maize, [National Museum of Anthropology of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Anthropology_(Mexico) "National Museum of Anthropology (Mexico)")

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
Maize [requires human intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultigen "Cultigen") for its propagation. The kernels of its naturally-propagating [teosinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte") ancestor fall off the cob on their own, while those of [domesticated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesticated "Domesticated") maize do not.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Benz_2001-49) All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. The oldest surviving maize types are those of the Mexican highlands. Maize spread from this region to the lowlands and over the Americas along two major paths.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27) The centre of domestication was most likely the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley of south-central Mexico.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50) Maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8000 years ago.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Pag%C3%A1n-Jim%C3%A9nezGuacham%C3%ADn-Tello2015-51) It reached lower Central America by 7,600 years ago, and the valleys of the Colombian [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") between 7,000 and 6,000 years ago.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50)

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
The earliest maize plants grew a single, small ear per plant.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Davidson_2014-6) The [Olmec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec "Olmec") and [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples") cultivated maize in numerous varieties throughout [Mesoamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica"); they cooked, ground and processed it through [nixtamalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization "Nixtamalization").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) By 3000 years ago, maize was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language, and myths.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)
The [Mapuche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapuche "Mapuche") people of [south-central Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zona_Sur "Zona Sur") cultivated maize along with [quinoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinoa "Quinoa") and [potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potatoes "Potatoes") in [pre-Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") times.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Dille2007-52) Before the expansion of the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire"), maize was traded and transported as far south as 40° S in Melinquina, [Lácar Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1car_Department "Lácar Department"), Argentina, probably brought across the Andes from Chile.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-PerezErre2011-53)

Almost any grocery store is filled with products made from corn, also known as maize, in every aisle: fresh corn, canned corn, corn cereal, taco shells, tortilla chips, popcorn, corn sweeteners in hundreds of products, corn fillers in pet food, in soaps and cosmetics, and the list goes on.
Maize is perhaps the most important plant ever domesticated by people, topping 1 billion tonnes produced in 2019, double that of rice, according to University of New Mexico Anthropology professor [Keith Prufer](http://www.unm.edu/~kmp/), principle investigator of a team that just released new research that sheds light on when people started eating maize.
The research, titled _[Early isotopic evidence for maize as a staple grain in the Americas](https://advances.sciencemag.org/content/6/23/eaba3245)_ and published by Prufer and his team in the journal Science Advances, reveals new information about when the now-ubiquitous maize became a key part of people’s diets. Until now, little was known about when humans living in the tropics of Central America first started eating corn. But the “unparalleled” discovery of remarkably well-preserved ancient human skeletons in Central American rock shelters has revealed when corn became a key part of people’s diet in the Americas.
[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8diGNcDPxLI)
“Today, much of the popularity of maize has to do with its high carbohydrate and protein value in animal feed and sugar content which makes it the preferred ingredient of many processed foods including sugary drinks. Traditionally it has also been used as a fermented drink in Mesoamerica.Given its humble beginnings 9,000 years ago in Mexico, understanding how it came to be the most dominant plant in the world benefits from deciphering what attracted people to this crop to begin with. Our paper is the first direct measure of the adoption of maize as a dietary staple in humans,” Prufer observed.
Prufer said the international team of researchers led by UNM and University of California, Santa Barbara is investigating the earliest humans in Central America and how they adapted over time to new and changing environments, and how those changes have affected human life histories and societies.
texts.1:
“One of the key issues for understanding these changes from an evolutionary perspective is to know what the change from hunting and gathers pathways to the development of agriculture looked like, and the pace and tempo of innovative new subsistence strategies," said Prufer."Food production and agriculture were among the most important cultural innovations in human history. Farming allowed us to live in larger groups, in the same location, and to develop permanent villages around food production."
"These changes ultimately led in the Maya area to the development of the Classic Period city-states of the Maya between 3,000 and 1,000 years ago. However, until this study, we did not know when early Mesoamericans first became farmers, or how quickly they accepted the new cultigen maize as a stable of their diet. Certainly, they were very successful in their previous foraging, hunting, and horticultural pursuits before farming, so it is of considerable interest to understand the timing and underlying processes."
Radiocarbon dating of the skeletal samples shows the transition from pre-maize hunter-gatherer diets, where people consumed wild plants and animals, to the introduction and increasing reliance on the corn. Maize made up less than 30 percent of people’s diets in the area by 4,700 years ago, rising to 70 percent 700 years later.
Maize was domesticated from teosinte, a wild grass growing in the lower reaches of the Balsas River Valley of Central Mexico, around 9,000 years ago. There is evidence maize was first cultivated in the Maya lowlands around 6,500 years ago, at about the same time that it appears along the Pacific coast of Mexico. But there is no evidence that maize was a staple grain at that time.
The first use of corn may have been for an early form of liquor.
“We hypothesize that maize stalk juice just may have been the original use of early domesticated maize plants, at a time when the cobs and seeds were essentially too small to be of much dietary significance. Humans are good at fermenting sugary liquids into alcoholic drinks.This changed as human selection of corn plants with larger and larger seeds coincided with genetic changes in the plants themselves, leading eventually to larger cobs, with more and larger seeds in more seed rows,” Prufer explained.
texts.2:
> _**“We did five years of fieldwork in two very remote rock shelter sites in the Bladen Nature Reserve in the Maya Mountains of Belize, a vast wilderness area that is a two-day walk from the nearest road. To work in this area we had to camp with no electricity, running water, or even cell service for a month at a time each year.”**_
To determine the presence of maize in the diet of the ancient individuals, Prufer and his colleagues measured the carbon isotopes in the bones and teeth of 52 skeletons. The study involved the remains of male and female adults and children providing a wholistic sample of the population. The oldest remains date from between 9,600 and 8,600 years ago and continues to about 1,000 years ago.
The analysis shows the oldest remains were people who ate wild plants, palms, fruits, and nuts found in tropical forests and savannahs, along with meat from hunting terrestrial animals.
By 4,700 years ago, diets had become more diverse, with some individuals showing the first consumption of maize. The isotopic signature of two young nursing infants shows that their mothers were consuming substantial amounts of maize. The results show an increasing consumption of maize over the next millennium as the population transitioned to sedentary farming.
Prufer noted, “We can directly observe in isotopes of bone how maize became a staple grain in the early populations we are studying. We know that people had been experimenting with the wild ancestor of maize, teocintle, and with the earliest early maize for thousands of years, but it does not appear to have been a staple grain until about 4000 [BP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Present). After that, people never stopped eating corn, leading it to become perhaps the most important food crop in the Americas, and then in the world.”
Excavations were directed by Prufer along with an international team of archaeologists, biologists, ecologists and geologists. Numerous UNM graduate and undergraduate students took part in the field research as well as collaborators with the protected area co-management team, a Belizean NGO the Ya’axche’ Conservation Trust.
texts.3:
Conditions weren’t easy for the excavation teams, Prufer noted: “We did five years of fieldwork in two very remote rock shelter sites in the [Bladen Nature Reserve](https://yaaxche.org/protecting-wild-places/bladen/) in the Maya Mountains of Belize, a vast wilderness area that is a two-day walk from the nearest road. To work in this area we had to camp with no electricity, running water, or even cell service for a month at a time each year.”
The analysis was conducted at Penn State University, UNM Center for Stable Isotopes, UCSB, and Exeter University in the UK. Prufer was the project director along with his colleague Doug Kennett from UCSB. The project was funded by the Alphawood Foundation and the National Science Foundation. The study was conducted by researchers from UNM, UCSB, Pennsylvania State University, University of Exeter, The US Army Central Identification Laboratory, University of Mississippi, Northern Arizona University, and the Ya’axche Conservation Trust in Belize.
Now that the research is published, the team will advance it to the next stage.
“New technologies allow us to look even deeper into molecular analysis through studies of ancient DNA and isotopic analysis of individual amino acids that are involved in turning food into building blocks of tissues and energy.We already have a Ph.D. students working on expanding our work to the next generation of analysis,” Prufer said.

## Description
Botanically, as in all grasses, it is a fruit, fused with the seed coat to form a [caryopsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryopsis "Caryopsis"))[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-4) when it is pollinated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Solaimalai_Anantharaju_2020_ch.6-3) A whole female inflorescence develops into an ear or [corncob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corncob "Corncob"), enveloped by multiple leafy layers or husks.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Solaimalai_Anantharaju_2020_ch.6-3) The ear leaf is the leaf most closely associated with a particular developing ear. This leaf and those above it contribute over three quarters of the carbohydrate ([starch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch")) that fills the grain.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-USA-IA-ext-fung-5)
The grains are usually yellow or white in modern varieties; other varieties have orange, red, brown, [blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_corn "Blue corn"), [purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_corn "Purple corn"), or black grains. They are arranged in 8 to 32 rows around the cob; there can be up to 1200 grains on a large cob.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Davidson_2014-6) Yellow maizes derive their color from [carotenoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carotenoid "Carotenoid"); red maizes are colored by [anthocyanins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthocyanin "Anthocyanin") and [phlobaphenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlobaphene "Phlobaphene"); and orange and green varieties may contain combinations of these pigments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Chatham_Paulsmeyer_Juvik_2019-7)
texts.10:
## Description
Maize has short-day [photoperiodism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoperiodism "Photoperiodism"), meaning that it requires nights of a certain length to flower. Flowering further requires [enough warm days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growing_degree_day "Growing degree day") above 10°C (50°F). The control of flowering is set genetically; the physiological mechanism involves the [phytochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytochrome "Phytochrome") system. Tropical cultivars can be problematic if grown in higher latitudes, as the longer days can make the plants grow tall instead of setting seed before winter comes. On the other hand, growing tall rapidly could be convenient for producing biofuel.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Solaimalai_Anantharaju_2020_ch.6-3)
Immature maize shoots accumulate a powerful antibiotic substance, 2,4-dihydroxy-7-methoxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one ([DIMBOA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DIMBOA "DIMBOA")), which provides a measure of protection against a wide range of pests.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Smith2012-8) Because of its shallow roots, maize is susceptible to droughts, intolerant of nutrient-deficient soils, and prone to being uprooted by severe winds.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-9)
The pollen is an [allergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allergen "Allergen"), but most of it falls within a few meters of the tassel and the risk is largely restricted to farm workers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-10)

## Genetics

## Genetics
Maize is [diploid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploid "Diploid") with 20 [chromosomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosome "Chromosome"). 83% of [allelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele "Allele") variation within the genome derives from its teosinte ancestors, primarily due to the freedom of _Zea_ species to [outcross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outcross "Outcross").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Back-to-the-Wild-11)[Barbara McClintock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_McClintock "Barbara McClintock") used maize to validate her [transposon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposon "Transposon") theory of "jumping genes", for which she won the 1983 [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-12) Maize remains an important [model organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_organism "Model organism") for genetics and [developmental biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developmental_biology "Developmental biology").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Strable_Scanlon_2009-13) The [MADS-box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MADS-box "MADS-box") motif is involved in the development of maize flowers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Friedman-et-al-2004-14)
texts.15:
## Genetics
The Maize Genetics and Genomics Database is funded by the [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture") (USDA) to support maize research.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-15) The [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") maintains a large collection of maize accessions tested and cataloged for insect resistance.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Breeding-Towards-16) In 2005, the U.S. [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), the USDA, and the [Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") formed a consortium to sequence the maize [genome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome"). The resulting [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") sequence data was deposited immediately into [GenBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GenBank "GenBank"), a public repository for genome-sequence data.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-17) Sequencing of the maize genome was completed in 2008.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-18) In 2009, the consortium published results of its sequencing effort.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-19) The genome, 85% of which is composed of [transposons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposon "Transposon"), contains 32,540 genes. Much of it has been duplicated and reshuffled by [helitrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helitron_(biology) "Helitron (biology)"), a group of [transposable elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposable_element "Transposable element") within maize's DNA.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-20)

## Taxonomy
### External phylogeny
The maize [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus")_Zea_ is relatively closely related to [sorghum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorghum "Sorghum"), both being in the [PACMAD clade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PACMAD_clade "PACMAD clade") of Old World grasses, and much more distantly to [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") and [wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheat "Wheat"), which are in the other major group of grasses, the [BOP clade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOP_clade "BOP clade"). It is closely related to _[Tripsacum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripsacum "Tripsacum")_, gamagrass.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Gaut_Le_Thierry_dEnnequin_Peek_Sawkins_2000-21)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Cornselection.jpg/250px-Cornselection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cornselection.jpg)
Teosinte (left), maize-teosinte hybrid (middle), maize (right)
Maize is the [domesticated variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_domestication "Crop domestication") of the four species of [teosintes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte"), which are its [crop wild relatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) Teosinte was likely used by hunter-gatherers because it added security to their food supply, being that it was adaptable to changes in climate and environment.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Lohse_Morgan_Jones_2022-2) The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the Russian botanist [Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Ivanovich_Vavilov "Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov") in 1931, and the American [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize")-winner [George Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Beadle "George Beadle") in 1932.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23):10 The two plants have dissimilar appearance, maize having a single tall stalk with multiple leaves and teosinte being a short, bushy plant.

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
The difference between the two is largely controlled by differences in just two genes, called grassy tillers-1 (_gt1_, [A0A317YEZ1](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/A0A317YEZ1)) and teosinte branched-1 (_tb1_, [Q93WI2](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q93WI2)).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) In the late 1930s, [Paul Mangelsdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Mangelsdorf "Paul Mangelsdorf") suggested that domesticated maize was the result of a hybridization event between an unknown wild maize and a species of _[Tripsacum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripsacum "Tripsacum")_, a related genus; this has been refuted by modern [genetic testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_testing "Genetic testing").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23)
texts.19:
## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
In 2004, [John Doebley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doebley "John Doebley") identified Balsas teosinte, _Zea mays_ subsp. _parviglumis_, native to the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley in Mexico's southwestern highlands, as the [crop wild relative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative") genetically most similar to modern maize.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Wu-et-al-2011-25) The middle part of the short Balsas River valley is the likely location of early domestication. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700 year old layer of deposits in a cave not far from [Iguala, Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguala,_Guerrero "Iguala, Guerrero").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) Doebley and colleagues showed in 2002 that maize had been domesticated only once, about 9,000 years ago, and then spread throughout the Americas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27)
texts.20:
## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
Maize pollen dated to 7,300 years ago from [San Andres, Tabasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andr%C3%A9s_(Mesoamerican_site) "San Andrés (Mesoamerican site)") has been found on the Caribbean coast.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) A primitive corn was being grown in southern Mexico, Central America, and northern South America 7,000 years ago. Archaeological remains of early maize ears, found at [Guila Naquitz Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guila_Naquitz_Cave "Guila Naquitz Cave") in the [Oaxaca Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca_Valley "Oaxaca Valley"), are roughly 6,250 years old; the oldest ears from caves near [Tehuacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehuac%C3%A1n,_Puebla "Tehuacán, Puebla"), Puebla, are 5,450 years old.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28)
texts.21:
## Taxonomy
### Spreading to the north
Around 4,500 years ago, maize began to spread to the north. Maize was first cultivated at several sites in New Mexico and Arizona about 4,100 years ago.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) During the first millennium AD, maize cultivation spread more widely in the areas north. In particular, the large-scale adoption of maize agriculture and consumption in eastern North America took place about A.D. 900. Native Americans cleared large forest and grassland areas for the new crop.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-29) The rise in maize cultivation 500 to 1,000 years ago in what is now the [southeastern U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_U.S. "Southeastern U.S.") corresponded with a decline of freshwater [mussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussel "Mussel"), which are very sensitive to environmental changes.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-30)
texts.22:
## Taxonomy
### Names
The name _maize_ derives from the Spanish form _maíz_ of the [Taíno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%ADno_language "Taíno language")_mahis_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-31) The Swedish botanist [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") used the common name maize as the species epithet in _Zea mays_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranum-32) The name _maize_ is preferred in formal, scientific, and international usage as a [common name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_name "Common name") because it refers specifically to this one grain, unlike _corn_, which has a complex variety of meanings that vary by context and geographic region.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) Most countries primarily use the term _maize_, and the name _corn_ is used mainly in the U.S.
texts.23:
## Taxonomy
### Names
and a handful of other English-speaking countries.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OxfordEncyclopedia-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Espinoza_2015-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-36) In countries that primarily use the term _maize_, the word _corn_ may denote any [cereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal "Cereal") crop, varying geographically with the local [staple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OED_corn-37) such as wheat in England and oats in Scotland or Ireland.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) The usage of _corn_ for maize started as a shortening of "[Indian corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_corn "Flint corn")" in 18th-century North America.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mencken-38)
The historian of food [Betty Fussell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Fussell "Betty Fussell") writes in an article on the history of the word _corn_ in North America that "[t]o say the word _corn_ is to plunge into the tragi-farcical mistranslations of language and history".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39) Similar to the British usage, the Spanish referred to maize as _panizo_, a generic term for cereal grains, as did Italians with the term _polenta_. The British later referred to maize as Turkey wheat, Turkey corn, or Indian corn; Fussell comments that "they meant not a place but a condition, a savage rather than a civilized grain".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)
texts.24:
## Taxonomy
### Names
International groups such as the [Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Agriculture_and_Bioscience_International "Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International") consider _maize_ the preferred common name.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-40) The word _maize_ is used by the UN's [Food and Agriculture Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-41) and in the names of the [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") of Mexico, the Indian Institute of Maize Research,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-42) the Maize Association of Australia,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-43) the National Maize Association of Nigeria,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-44) the National Maize Association of Ghana,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-45) the Maize Trust of South Africa,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-46) and the Zimbabwe Seed Maize Association.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Rusike_Donovan_1995-47) In the United States, _maize_ can be used interchangeably with the term _corn_.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-48)

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
Maize [requires human intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultigen "Cultigen") for its propagation. The kernels of its naturally-propagating [teosinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte") ancestor fall off the cob on their own, while those of [domesticated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesticated "Domesticated") maize do not.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Benz_2001-49) All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. The oldest surviving maize types are those of the Mexican highlands. Maize spread from this region to the lowlands and over the Americas along two major paths.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27) The centre of domestication was most likely the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley of south-central Mexico.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50) Maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8000 years ago.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Pag%C3%A1n-Jim%C3%A9nezGuacham%C3%ADn-Tello2015-51) It reached lower Central America by 7,600 years ago, and the valleys of the Colombian [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") between 7,000 and 6,000 years ago.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50)
texts.27:
## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
The earliest maize plants grew a single, small ear per plant.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Davidson_2014-6) The [Olmec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec "Olmec") and [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples") cultivated maize in numerous varieties throughout [Mesoamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica"); they cooked, ground and processed it through [nixtamalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization "Nixtamalization").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) By 3000 years ago, maize was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language, and myths.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)
The [Mapuche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapuche "Mapuche") people of [south-central Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zona_Sur "Zona Sur") cultivated maize along with [quinoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinoa "Quinoa") and [potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potatoes "Potatoes") in [pre-Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") times.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Dille2007-52) Before the expansion of the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire"), maize was traded and transported as far south as 40° S in Melinquina, [Lácar Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1car_Department "Lácar Department"), Argentina, probably brought across the Andes from Chile.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-PerezErre2011-53)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Cornselection.jpg/250px-Cornselection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cornselection.jpg)
Teosinte (left), maize-teosinte hybrid (middle), maize (right)
Maize is the [domesticated variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_domestication "Crop domestication") of the four species of [teosintes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte"), which are its [crop wild relatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) Teosinte was likely used by hunter-gatherers because it added security to their food supply, being that it was adaptable to changes in climate and environment.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Lohse_Morgan_Jones_2022-2) The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the Russian botanist [Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Ivanovich_Vavilov "Nikolai Ivanovich Vavilov") in 1931, and the American [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize")-winner [George Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Beadle "George Beadle") in 1932.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23):10 The two plants have dissimilar appearance, maize having a single tall stalk with multiple leaves and teosinte being a short, bushy plant.

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
The difference between the two is largely controlled by differences in just two genes, called grassy tillers-1 (_gt1_, [A0A317YEZ1](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/A0A317YEZ1)) and teosinte branched-1 (_tb1_, [Q93WI2](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/Q93WI2)).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-corn-22) In the late 1930s, [Paul Mangelsdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Mangelsdorf "Paul Mangelsdorf") suggested that domesticated maize was the result of a hybridization event between an unknown wild maize and a species of _[Tripsacum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripsacum "Tripsacum")_, a related genus; this has been refuted by modern [genetic testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_testing "Genetic testing").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-wilkes-23)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
In 2004, [John Doebley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doebley "John Doebley") identified Balsas teosinte, _Zea mays_ subsp. _parviglumis_, native to the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley in Mexico's southwestern highlands, as the [crop wild relative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_wild_relative "Crop wild relative") genetically most similar to modern maize.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Wu-et-al-2011-25) The middle part of the short Balsas River valley is the likely location of early domestication. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700 year old layer of deposits in a cave not far from [Iguala, Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguala,_Guerrero "Iguala, Guerrero").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) Doebley and colleagues showed in 2002 that maize had been domesticated only once, about 9,000 years ago, and then spread throughout the Americas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27)

## Taxonomy
### Maize and teosinte
Maize pollen dated to 7,300 years ago from [San Andres, Tabasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andr%C3%A9s_(Mesoamerican_site) "San Andrés (Mesoamerican site)") has been found on the Caribbean coast.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranere-26) A primitive corn was being grown in southern Mexico, Central America, and northern South America 7,000 years ago. Archaeological remains of early maize ears, found at [Guila Naquitz Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guila_Naquitz_Cave "Guila Naquitz Cave") in the [Oaxaca Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca_Valley "Oaxaca Valley"), are roughly 6,250 years old; the oldest ears from caves near [Tehuacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehuac%C3%A1n,_Puebla "Tehuacán, Puebla"), Puebla, are 5,450 years old.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28)

## Taxonomy
### Spreading to the north
Around 4,500 years ago, maize began to spread to the north. Maize was first cultivated at several sites in New Mexico and Arizona about 4,100 years ago.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) During the first millennium AD, maize cultivation spread more widely in the areas north. In particular, the large-scale adoption of maize agriculture and consumption in eastern North America took place about A.D. 900. Native Americans cleared large forest and grassland areas for the new crop.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-29) The rise in maize cultivation 500 to 1,000 years ago in what is now the [southeastern U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_U.S. "Southeastern U.S.") corresponded with a decline of freshwater [mussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussel "Mussel"), which are very sensitive to environmental changes.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-30)

## Taxonomy
### Names
The name _maize_ derives from the Spanish form _maíz_ of the [Taíno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%ADno_language "Taíno language")_mahis_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-31) The Swedish botanist [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") used the common name maize as the species epithet in _Zea mays_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ranum-32) The name _maize_ is preferred in formal, scientific, and international usage as a [common name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_name "Common name") because it refers specifically to this one grain, unlike _corn_, which has a complex variety of meanings that vary by context and geographic region.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) Most countries primarily use the term _maize_, and the name _corn_ is used mainly in the U.S.

## Taxonomy
### Names
and a handful of other English-speaking countries.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OxfordEncyclopedia-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Espinoza_2015-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-36) In countries that primarily use the term _maize_, the word _corn_ may denote any [cereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal "Cereal") crop, varying geographically with the local [staple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-OED_corn-37) such as wheat in England and oats in Scotland or Ireland.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ensminger-33) The usage of _corn_ for maize started as a shortening of "[Indian corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_corn "Flint corn")" in 18th-century North America.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mencken-38)
The historian of food [Betty Fussell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Fussell "Betty Fussell") writes in an article on the history of the word _corn_ in North America that "[t]o say the word _corn_ is to plunge into the tragi-farcical mistranslations of language and history".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39) Similar to the British usage, the Spanish referred to maize as _panizo_, a generic term for cereal grains, as did Italians with the term _polenta_. The British later referred to maize as Turkey wheat, Turkey corn, or Indian corn; Fussell comments that "they meant not a place but a condition, a savage rather than a civilized grain".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)

## Taxonomy
### Names
International groups such as the [Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Agriculture_and_Bioscience_International "Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International") consider _maize_ the preferred common name.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-40) The word _maize_ is used by the UN's [Food and Agriculture Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-41) and in the names of the [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") of Mexico, the Indian Institute of Maize Research,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-42) the Maize Association of Australia,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-43) the National Maize Association of Nigeria,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-44) the National Maize Association of Ghana,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-45) the Maize Trust of South Africa,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-46) and the Zimbabwe Seed Maize Association.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Rusike_Donovan_1995-47) In the United States, _maize_ can be used interchangeably with the term _corn_.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-48)

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg/250px-Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museo_Nacional_de_Antropolog%C3%ADa_-_MA%C3%8DZ.jpg)
Ancient Mesoamerican relief sculpture of maize, [National Museum of Anthropology of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Anthropology_(Mexico) "National Museum of Anthropology (Mexico)")

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
Maize [requires human intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultigen "Cultigen") for its propagation. The kernels of its naturally-propagating [teosinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teosinte "Teosinte") ancestor fall off the cob on their own, while those of [domesticated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesticated "Domesticated") maize do not.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Benz_2001-49) All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. The oldest surviving maize types are those of the Mexican highlands. Maize spread from this region to the lowlands and over the Americas along two major paths.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Mat-27) The centre of domestication was most likely the [Balsas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balsas_River "Balsas River") valley of south-central Mexico.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50) Maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8000 years ago.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Pag%C3%A1n-Jim%C3%A9nezGuacham%C3%ADn-Tello2015-51) It reached lower Central America by 7,600 years ago, and the valleys of the Colombian [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") between 7,000 and 6,000 years ago.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Piperno-2011-50)

## Cultivation
### Pre-Columbian development
The earliest maize plants grew a single, small ear per plant.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Davidson_2014-6) The [Olmec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec "Olmec") and [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples") cultivated maize in numerous varieties throughout [Mesoamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica"); they cooked, ground and processed it through [nixtamalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization "Nixtamalization").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Roney_2009-28) By 3000 years ago, maize was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language, and myths.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Fussell1999-39)
The [Mapuche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapuche "Mapuche") people of [south-central Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zona_Sur "Zona Sur") cultivated maize along with [quinoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinoa "Quinoa") and [potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potatoes "Potatoes") in [pre-Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") times.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Dille2007-52) Before the expansion of the [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire"), maize was traded and transported as far south as 40° S in Melinquina, [Lácar Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1car_Department "Lácar Department"), Argentina, probably brought across the Andes from Chile.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-PerezErre2011-53)

## Cultivation
### Columbian exchange
[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/The_Florentine_Codex-_Agriculture.tiff/lossy-page1-250px-The_Florentine_Codex-_Agriculture.tiff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Florentine_Codex-_Agriculture.tiff)
Cultivation of maize, illustrated in the 16th-century _[Florentine Codex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florentine\_Codex "Florentine Codex")_
After the arrival of Europeans in 1492, Spanish settlers consumed maize, and explorers and traders [carried it back to Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_Exchange "Columbian Exchange"). Spanish settlers much preferred [wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheat "Wheat") bread to maize. Maize flour could not be substituted for wheat for communion bread, since in [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") belief at that time only wheat could undergo [transubstantiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transubstantiation "Transubstantiation") and be transformed into the body of Christ.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Earle_2012-54)

## Cultivation
### Columbian exchange
Maize spread to the rest of the world because of its ability to grow in diverse climates. It was cultivated in Spain just a few decades after Columbus's voyages and then spread to Italy, [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa"), the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") and elsewhere.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Earle_2012-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Salazar2016-55) By the 17th century, it was a common peasant food in Southern Europe. By the 18th century, it was the chief food of the southern French and Italian peasantry, especially as [polenta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polenta "Polenta") in Italy.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-56)

## Cultivation
### Columbian exchange
When maize was introduced into Western farming systems, it was welcomed for its productivity. However, a widespread problem of malnutrition soon arose wherever it had become a [staple food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-pellagra_mystery-57) Indigenous Americans had learned to soak maize in [alkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali "Alkali")-water–made with ashes and [lime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_oxide "Calcium oxide")–since at least 1200–1500 BC, creating the process of [nixtamalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization "Nixtamalization"). They did this to liberate the corn hulls, but coincidentally it also liberated the B-vitamin [niacin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niacin_(nutrient) "Niacin (nutrient)"), the lack of which caused [pellagra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellagra "Pellagra").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-StallerCarrasco2009-58) Once alkali processing and dietary variety were understood and applied, pellagra disappeared in the developed world. The development of high-[lysine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysine "Lysine") maize and the promotion of a more balanced diet have contributed to its demise. Pellagra still exists in food-poor areas and refugee camps where people survive on donated maize.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Thompson2016-59)

## Cultivation
### Conventional breeding
Maize breeding in prehistory resulted in large plants producing large ears. Modern [breeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_breeding "Plant breeding") began with individuals who selected highly productive varieties in their fields and then sold seed to other farmers. James L. Reid was one of the earliest and most successful, developing Reid's Yellow Dent in the 1860s. These early efforts were based on [mass selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selection_methods_in_plant_breeding_based_on_mode_of_reproduction "Selection methods in plant breeding based on mode of reproduction") (a row of plants is grown from seeds of one parent), and the choosing of plants after pollination (which means that only the female parents are known). Later breeding efforts included ear to row selection (C. G. Hopkins c. 1896), hybrids made from selected [inbred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbred "Inbred") lines (G. H. Shull, 1909), and the highly successful [double cross hybrids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_cross_hybrid "Double cross hybrid") using four inbred lines ([D. F. Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_F._Jones "Donald F. Jones") c. 1918, 1922). University-supported breeding programs were especially important in developing and introducing modern hybrids.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Jugen-60)
Since the 1940s, the best strains of maize have been first-generation hybrids made from inbred strains that have been optimized for specific traits, such as yield, nutrition, drought, pest and disease tolerance. Both conventional cross-breeding and genetic engineering have succeeded in increasing output and reducing the need for cropland, pesticides, water and fertilizer. There is conflicting evidence to support the hypothesis that maize yield potential has increased over the past few decades. This suggests that changes in yield potential are associated with leaf angle, lodging resistance, tolerance of high plant density, disease/pest tolerance, and other agronomic traits rather than increase of yield potential per individual plant.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-61)

## Cultivation
### Conventional breeding
Certain varieties of maize have been bred to produce many ears; these are the source of the "[baby corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_corn "Baby corn")" used as a vegetable in [Asian cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_cuisine "Asian cuisine").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Lopes_N%C3%B3brega_Pacheco_Cruz-Silva_2016-63) A fast-flowering variety named mini-maize was developed to aid scientific research, as multiple generations can be obtained in a single year.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-64) One strain called olotón has evolved a symbiotic relationship with [nitrogen-fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_fixation "Nitrogen fixation") microbes, which provides the plant with 29%–82% of its nitrogen.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-65) The [International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Maize_and_Wheat_Improvement_Center "International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center") (CIMMYT) operates a conventional breeding program to provide optimized strains. The program began in the 1980s.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-cimmyt-66) Hybrid seeds are distributed in Africa by its Drought Tolerant Maize for Africa project.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-67)

## Cultivation
### Conventional breeding
Tropical [landraces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landrace "Landrace") remain an important and underused source of resistance alleles – both those [for disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_disease_resistance "Plant disease resistance") and [for herbivores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_defense_against_herbivory "Plant defense against herbivory"). Such alleles can then be [introgressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introgressed "Introgressed") into productive varieties.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Chakradhar-et-al-2017-68) Rare alleles for this purpose were discovered by Dao and Sood, both in 2014.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Chakradhar-et-al-2017-68) In 2018, Zerka Rashid of CIMMYT used its [association mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_mapping "Association mapping") panel, developed for tropical drought tolerance traits. to find new [genomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome") regions providing [sorghum downy mildew resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorghum_downy_mildew_resistance "Sorghum downy mildew resistance"), and to further characterize known [differentially methylated regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentially_methylated_region "Differentially methylated region").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Rashid_Singh_Vemuri_Zaidi_2018-69)

## Cultivation
### Genetic engineering
[Genetically modified maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetically_modified_maize "Genetically modified maize") was one of the 26 [genetically engineered food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetically_engineered_food "Genetically engineered food") crops grown commercially in 2016.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-James-2016-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-71) The vast majority of this is [Bt maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bt_maize "Bt maize"). Genetically modified maize has been grown since 1997 in the United States and Canada;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-Ostry-et-al-2015-72) by 2016, 92% of the U.S. maize crop was genetically modified.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-James-2016-70) As of 2011, herbicide-tolerant maize and insect-resistant maize varieties were each grown in over 20 countries.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-73)
In September 2000, up to $50 million worth of food products were recalled due to the presence of [Starlink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/StarLink_corn_recall "StarLink corn recall") genetically modified corn, which had been approved only for animal consumption.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-74)

## Cultivation
### Growing
Because it is cold-intolerant, in the [temperate zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate") maize must be planted in the spring. Its [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root "Root") system is generally shallow, so the plant is dependent on soil moisture. As a plant that uses [C 4 carbon fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C4_carbon_fixation "C4 carbon fixation"), maize is a considerably more water-efficient crop than plants that use [C 3 carbon fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_carbon_fixation "C3 carbon fixation") such as [alfalfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfalfa "Alfalfa") and [soybeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soybean "Soybean"). Maize is most sensitive to drought at the time of silk emergence, when the flowers are ready for pollination. In the United States, a good harvest was traditionally predicted if the maize was "knee-high by the [Fourth of July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Day_(United_States) "Independence Day (United States)")", although modern [hybrids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_(biology) "Hybrid (biology)") generally exceed this growth rate. Maize used for [silage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silage "Silage") is harvested while the plant is green and the fruit immature. Sweet corn is harvested in the "milk stage", after pollination but before starch has formed, between late summer and early to mid-autumn. Field maize is left in the field until very late in the autumn to thoroughly dry the grain, and may, in fact, sometimes not be harvested until winter or even early spring. The importance of sufficient soil moisture is shown in many parts of Africa, where periodic [drought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drought "Drought") regularly causes maize crop failure and consequent [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine"). Although it is grown mainly in wet, hot climates, it can thrive in cold, hot, dry or wet conditions, meaning that it is an extremely versatile crop.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize#cite_note-75)

Source: https://news.unm.edu/news/releases-20200601-6803126
Title: UNM researchers document the first use of maize in Mesoamerica
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Almost any grocery store is filled with products made from corn, also known as maize, in every aisle: fresh corn, canned corn, corn cereal, taco shells, tortilla chips, popcorn, corn sweeteners in hundreds of products, corn fillers in pet food, in soaps and cosmetics, and the list goes on.
Maize is perhaps the most important plant ever domesticated by people, topping 1 billion tonnes produced in 2019, double that of rice, according to University of New Mexico Anthropology professor [Keith Prufer](http://www.unm.edu/~kmp/), principle investigator of a team that just released new research that sheds light on when people started eating maize.
The research, titled _[Early isotopic evidence for maize as a staple grain in the Americas](https://advances.sciencemag.org/content/6/23/eaba3245)_ and published by Prufer and his team in the journal Science Advances, reveals new information about when the now-ubiquitous maize became a key part of people’s diets. Until now, little was known about when humans living in the tropics of Central America first started eating corn. But the “unparalleled” discovery of remarkably well-preserved ancient human skeletons in Central American rock shelters has revealed when corn became a key part of people’s diet in the Americas.
[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8diGNcDPxLI)
“Today, much of the popularity of maize has to do with its high carbohydrate and protein value in animal feed and sugar content which makes it the preferred ingredient of many processed foods including sugary drinks. Traditionally it has also been used as a fermented drink in Mesoamerica.Given its humble beginnings 9,000 years ago in Mexico, understanding how it came to be the most dominant plant in the world benefits from deciphering what attracted people to this crop to begin with. Our paper is the first direct measure of the adoption of maize as a dietary staple in humans,” Prufer observed.
Prufer said the international team of researchers led by UNM and University of California, Santa Barbara is investigating the earliest humans in Central America and how they adapted over time to new and changing environments, and how those changes have affected human life histories and societies.

“One of the key issues for understanding these changes from an evolutionary perspective is to know what the change from hunting and gathers pathways to the development of agriculture looked like, and the pace and tempo of innovative new subsistence strategies," said Prufer."Food production and agriculture were among the most important cultural innovations in human history. Farming allowed us to live in larger groups, in the same location, and to develop permanent villages around food production."
"These changes ultimately led in the Maya area to the development of the Classic Period city-states of the Maya between 3,000 and 1,000 years ago. However, until this study, we did not know when early Mesoamericans first became farmers, or how quickly they accepted the new cultigen maize as a stable of their diet. Certainly, they were very successful in their previous foraging, hunting, and horticultural pursuits before farming, so it is of considerable interest to understand the timing and underlying processes."
Radiocarbon dating of the skeletal samples shows the transition from pre-maize hunter-gatherer diets, where people consumed wild plants and animals, to the introduction and increasing reliance on the corn. Maize made up less than 30 percent of people’s diets in the area by 4,700 years ago, rising to 70 percent 700 years later.
Maize was domesticated from teosinte, a wild grass growing in the lower reaches of the Balsas River Valley of Central Mexico, around 9,000 years ago. There is evidence maize was first cultivated in the Maya lowlands around 6,500 years ago, at about the same time that it appears along the Pacific coast of Mexico. But there is no evidence that maize was a staple grain at that time.
The first use of corn may have been for an early form of liquor.
“We hypothesize that maize stalk juice just may have been the original use of early domesticated maize plants, at a time when the cobs and seeds were essentially too small to be of much dietary significance. Humans are good at fermenting sugary liquids into alcoholic drinks.This changed as human selection of corn plants with larger and larger seeds coincided with genetic changes in the plants themselves, leading eventually to larger cobs, with more and larger seeds in more seed rows,” Prufer explained.

> _**“We did five years of fieldwork in two very remote rock shelter sites in the Bladen Nature Reserve in the Maya Mountains of Belize, a vast wilderness area that is a two-day walk from the nearest road. To work in this area we had to camp with no electricity, running water, or even cell service for a month at a time each year.”**_
To determine the presence of maize in the diet of the ancient individuals, Prufer and his colleagues measured the carbon isotopes in the bones and teeth of 52 skeletons. The study involved the remains of male and female adults and children providing a wholistic sample of the population. The oldest remains date from between 9,600 and 8,600 years ago and continues to about 1,000 years ago.
The analysis shows the oldest remains were people who ate wild plants, palms, fruits, and nuts found in tropical forests and savannahs, along with meat from hunting terrestrial animals.
By 4,700 years ago, diets had become more diverse, with some individuals showing the first consumption of maize. The isotopic signature of two young nursing infants shows that their mothers were consuming substantial amounts of maize. The results show an increasing consumption of maize over the next millennium as the population transitioned to sedentary farming.
Prufer noted, “We can directly observe in isotopes of bone how maize became a staple grain in the early populations we are studying. We know that people had been experimenting with the wild ancestor of maize, teocintle, and with the earliest early maize for thousands of years, but it does not appear to have been a staple grain until about 4000 [BP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Present). After that, people never stopped eating corn, leading it to become perhaps the most important food crop in the Americas, and then in the world.”
Excavations were directed by Prufer along with an international team of archaeologists, biologists, ecologists and geologists. Numerous UNM graduate and undergraduate students took part in the field research as well as collaborators with the protected area co-management team, a Belizean NGO the Ya’axche’ Conservation Trust.

Conditions weren’t easy for the excavation teams, Prufer noted: “We did five years of fieldwork in two very remote rock shelter sites in the [Bladen Nature Reserve](https://yaaxche.org/protecting-wild-places/bladen/) in the Maya Mountains of Belize, a vast wilderness area that is a two-day walk from the nearest road. To work in this area we had to camp with no electricity, running water, or even cell service for a month at a time each year.”
The analysis was conducted at Penn State University, UNM Center for Stable Isotopes, UCSB, and Exeter University in the UK. Prufer was the project director along with his colleague Doug Kennett from UCSB. The project was funded by the Alphawood Foundation and the National Science Foundation. The study was conducted by researchers from UNM, UCSB, Pennsylvania State University, University of Exeter, The US Army Central Identification Laboratory, University of Mississippi, Northern Arizona University, and the Ya’axche Conservation Trust in Belize.
Now that the research is published, the team will advance it to the next stage.
“New technologies allow us to look even deeper into molecular analysis through studies of ancient DNA and isotopic analysis of individual amino acids that are involved in turning food into building blocks of tissues and energy.We already have a Ph.D. students working on expanding our work to the next generation of analysis,” Prufer said.
