### Maize in Mexico and Central America
Scientists think that maize began the process of domestication as long as 9000 years ago, when people in Mesoamerica began cultivating its ancestor, Balsas teosinte. The oldest maize pollen, about 8700 years old, comes from the Balsas Valley of Mexico, which is thought to have been the cradle of maize domestication. Additional maize pollen that is more than 7000 years old has been discovered in Tabasco, Mexico, and Panama. While the oldest maize cobs are from Peru, maize cobs that are more than 6000 years old are known from Oaxaca, Mexico. Additional maize cobs that are more than 4000 years old (the oldest is about 5900 years old) have been collected from other sites in Puebla and Tamaulipas, Mexico, as well as from the El Gigante rockshelter in Honduras.
Despite this evidence, analysis of human remains from Mesoamerica indicates that maize only became a significant part of some peoples' diets between about 4700 and 4000 years ago, shifting to a dietary staple after 4000 years ago.
* * *
[Learn more about maize domestication](https://evolution.earthathome.org/grasses/andropogoneae/maize-domestication)

### Maize in Mexico and Central America
#### Maize in past Mesoamerican cultures
The Olmec civilization (1200 to 400 BC), which was located in the region of modern-day Tabasco and Veracruz, southeastern Mexico, initially flourished without relying heavily on maize as a dietary staple. About 3000 years ago (900 BC), maize began to become a much more important part of the Olmec diet and culture.
The Mayan Civilization, which had its peak from around 250 AD to 950 AD, was centered in the same region as the Olmec civilization. Maize was so important to the ancient Mayans that it had spiritual and religious significance. According to Mayan legends, humans were created from maize. Many other Mayan legends revolve around maize, and images of maize have been found on Mayan artifacts, murals, and hieroglyphs. Key Mayan gods include the Tonsured Maize God and the Foliated Maize God. The Tonsured God’s head is shaved to represent a maize cob, with a small crest of hair to represent the tassel. The Foliated Maize God, on the other hand, symbolizes a still young, tender, and green maize ear.
* * *

### Maize in Mexico and Central America
#### Maize in past Mesoamerican cultures
Figure of the Young Maize Deity of the Maya, ca. 900s AD, in three views.[Left photo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Young_Corn_God_MET_DT9946.jpg), [center photo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Young_Corn_God_MET_DT9945.jpg), and [right photo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Young_Corn_God_MET_DT9945.jpg) by the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Wikimedia Commons, [Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en)).
* * *
Later, the Aztec civilization (about 1345 to 1521 AD), another civilization located in southern Mexico, also had maize dieties. Chicomecóatl (Seven Snake, goddess of mature maize) is depicted wearing a large headdress with rosettes and holding ears of maize. Other maize dieties include Xilonen, a goddess who represents young maize, and Cinteotl, a maize god.
The Aztec Empire came to an end in the 1500s, with the arrival of Spanish conquistadors led by Hernán Cortés. Aztec (or Nahua) society, including the maize deities and the use of maize, was later documented in the extensive _Florentine Codex_ assembled by Spanish priest Bernadino de Sahagún from 1540 to 1585 with the help of Nahua students.

texts.6:
### Maize in Mexico and Central America
#### Mexican and Central American food traditions
A diversity of varieties (called**landraces)** of maize are cultivated in Mexico and Central America, with the most (more than 60) known from Mexico.
Traditionally in Mesoamerica, and continuing today in the region, maize kernels were treating using a process called **nixtamalization**. The term "nixtamalization" comes from the Nahuatl word _nextamalli_, a word for limewater-treated maize kernels. During nixtamalization, maize kernels are steeped in limewater (alkaline water), which causes the outer walls of the kernels to separate from the grain, kills the embryos, and also frees niacin in the grain. The process changes the flavor of the kernels and also improves their storage life and nutritional value. These treated kernels can ground to make _**masa**_, the dough used to make a variety of foods, like gorditas and tortillas. Some researchers have speculated that nixtamalization is the reason that **pellagra**, a disease caused by niacin (vitamin B 3) deficiency that occurs in people with heavily maize-based diets lacking other sources of niacin, was not prevalent in Mesoamerica.
Many other types of food are made from maize in Mexico and Central America, including _**arepas**_ (fried cakes made of maize flour, discussed further below), and **_chorreadas_**(maize pancakes).

A person, mostly out of frame, is stirring the maize with a wooden spoon. The spoon has a white stain on it near the level of the pot, perhaps caused by the added lime. Cement blocks, plastic bottles, and other debris can be seen in the background.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Nixtamalization-maize-EOrchardsonCIMMTY-2000px.jpg)

### Maize in South America
Maize has long been cultivated in northern South America and may have reached the continent by 7000 years ago. Some of the oldest popcorn ever found, dating to about 6800 to 6500 years ago, was discovered in coastal Peru. Depictions of maize appear on ancient artifacts, like those from the Nazca Culture (northwestern South America, ca. 200 BC to 600 AD) and Moche Culture (coastal Peru, ca. 1 to 700 AD). Many varieties of maize continue to be grown in the Andes today.
* * *
![Image 8: 2-panel figure showing photos of ancient ceramics from Peru featuring maize. Panel 1: A vessel shaped like a stalk of maize with two ears. Panel 2: Vessel shaped like a rodent nibbling on an ear of maize.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Nazca-moche-maize-pottery-2000px.jpg)

texts.18:
### Maize in North America north of Mexico
#### Maize in the East
The earliest clear evidence for maize in eastern North America are kernels that are about 2,000 years old from the Holding Site near St. Louis, Missouri. Slightly younger remains are known from two other sites, one in Tennessee (about 1800 years old) and one in Ohio (about 1700 years old). The conversion of maize into a staple crop in the East, however, took at least 1000 years and coincided with the rise of Mississippian Culture.
Agriculture was a large part of Mississippian Culture, which was centered in the region now encompassed by the eastern United States. The Mississippian Culture began to flourish during a warm interval that began about 950 AD, which also saw expansion of and heavier reliance on agriculture to provide food. The peoples of the Mississippian Culture cultivated the three sisters of maize, beans, and squash. They also built major settlements, the biggest of which was Cahokia, located in southern Illinois, U.S.A.
While the largest Mississippian settlements had been abandoned, Mississippian agricultural traditions and smaller settlements were still present when Spanish explorers came into direct contact with the Native Peoples of the Southeast in the 1500s. The Native Peoples of this region typically ground their maize using wood mortars and pestles, rather than the stone mano and matate used in the Southwest and Mesoamerica. Many Native Peoples of the Southeast celebrated (and continue to celebrate) the Green Corn Dance or Green Corn Ceremony, an important ceremony of renewal.

texts.21:
### Maize in North America north of Mexico
#### North American (north of Mexico) food traditions
Once many Peoples in North America began to rely on agriculture to supply a substantial portion of their food, maize became very important in their diets. Some varieties of maize were traditionally grown in North America, like Hopi Blue Corn from the Southwest, Cherokee White Eagle from the Southeast, and Seneca Red Stalker from the Northeast.
* * *
![Image 25: Photograph of Cherokee White Eagle maize kernels. The photo shows maize kernels in a blue-patterned bowl. The kernels are purple and white in color.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Cherokee-white-eagle-corn-LanceCheung-USDA-2000px.jpg)
* * *
In North America north of Mexico, maize was cooked and eaten fresh, dried and stored, and ground into corn meal, corn flour, or, in the Southeast, ground into corn **grits**(course-ground maize kernels that may have been nixtamalized). **Cornbread**, another characteristic food of the Southeast, also has its roots in Native American cuisine.
One distinctive use for maize was to make a dish called **succotash**, a maize-based stew that originated in the region of present-day New England and typically includes beans and other ingredients. In the Southeast, some Native Americas Peoples (like the Cherokee, Creek, and Seminole) made **sofkee**. Sofkee is a type of maize soup typically prepared with lye made from wood ash. Peoples of North America north of Mexico also prepared nixtamalized maize, eating it in the form of **hominy**, which may have been used as whole or ground kernels.
One of the maize-based foods from the Southwest is **piki**, a Hopi flat bread made from maize flour, ash, and water that is prepared for special occasions.
* * *
![Image 26: Photograph of a meal at a restaurant in Atlanta, Georgia, U.S.A. The photo shows a round white plate with pieces of breaded, fried chicken, a bowl of breaded, fried okra, and a bowl of grits sitting on it. ](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Chicken-grits-okra-Atlanta-Georgia-DJLamar-2000px.jpg)

texts.23:
### Maize as a world crop
Today, maize is the most widely grown crop in the Americas, with 70 to 100 million acres grown annually in the U.S. alone, accounting for about 30% of the all maize grown in the world. It is a versatile crop, and can be grown in a number of different environments; it is grown on every continent except Antarctica. Maize is higher yielding than many other grains; its average yield is 160 bushels per acre but it can reach over 300 bushels per acre (27 tons per hectare), making it less expensive to grow (relative to yield) than other grains. Together with wheat and rice, maize is one of the three most important grain crops in the world.
* * *
![Image 29: World map showing maize production in 2020. Countries are shaded lighter green to indicate less production, darker green to indicate more production. The top producers (dark green countries) are the U.S.A., Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, Ukraine, India, and China.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Maize-global-production-2020-2000px.jpg)

texts.24:
### Maize as a world crop
#### Introduction of maize outside of the Americas
The first known contact that Europeans had with maize was through Christopher Columbus in the late 1400s, who encountered the plant in Caribbean, and brought seeds back to Europe in 1493. In fact, the word maize is taken from the Taíno language, then spoken by the Taíno People of the Caribbean.
The plants that produced the seeds the Columbus brought back to Europe were not selected for the more temperate climates of eastern and northern Europe and cultivation in Europe was limited. Sometime in the early 1500s, seeds or plants from further north in North America were introduced to Europe. These varieties were selected for cooler climates, allowing maize to be successfully cultivated further north in Europe. Maize also reached China by the 1500s, Africa by the 1600s, and India by the 1700s or earlier. Maize was introduced to these regions by European traders and colonizers and/or by overland spread from regions where maize had already been adopted.
* * *
![Image 30: Photo of a still life painting feature an ear of maize. The image shows a large blue bowl decorated with flowers and filled with grapes and peaches. A bunch of grapes, an ear of yellow maize, and other fruits (maybe plums) sit on a table in front of the bowl. A smaller bowl of red fruits sits to the right of the painting.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Still-life-painting-maize-JacobvanEs-web.jpg)

texts.25:
### Maize as a world crop
#### Pellagra
Maize was quickly taken up as a staple crop in many regions. It had the advantages that it provided many calories per plant, the kernels could be dried and stored for long periods of time, and the kernels were relatively easy to process. However, widespread adoption of maize had downsides. One of these was outbreaks of pellagra, a disease caused by niacin (vitamin B 3) deficiency. Symptoms of pellagra include skin lesions that develop on areas of the body that are exposed to the sun (like the hands and upper chest), gingivitis and a swollen tongue, diarrhea, and dementia. In severe cases, people die of disease. In the past, people suffering from dementia caused by pellagra were sent to asylums.
* * *
![Image 31: Two-panel image showing plates illustrating pellagra symptoms from a book published in 1814. Panel 1: Illustrations of two hands showing skin with rashes or plaques. Panel 2: Image of a person's neck and chest showing spotting, particularly on the lower neck and upper chest, indicating pellagra.](https://evolution.earthathome.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Pellagra-symptoms-DiVincenzioChiarugi-2000px.jpg)
Illustrations of symptoms of pellagra affecting the skin of the hands, chest, and neck of sufferers. Pellagra causes rashes and plaques to develop on sun-exposed skin.[Images from _Saggio di ricerche sulla pellagra_ by Di Vincenzio Chiarugi, 1814 (Wellcome Collection, public domain)](https://wellcomecollection.org/works/sm6f6dmf).
* * *
Pellagra sufferers were often poor with a diet that had limited variety, either seasonally or year-round. Many people with maize-based diets that lack other sources of niacin developed pellagra when maize was adopted as a staple crop. Pellagra was once common in Egypt, Europe, and the southeastern United States, and still occurs in some areas of sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. Some researchers think that, historically, nutritional problems developed in these populations because they did not nixtamalize maize. Nixtamalization increases the amount of niacin available in maize kernels, making them more nutritious. Other practices, like refining maize (removing the bran and germ), can further reduce its nutritional value.
texts.26:
### Maize as a world crop
#### Pellagra
Pellagra was first documented in Europe in the early 1700s, and a major treatise was written on it in the late 1700s. Nevertheless, the cause of the disease was not understood for more than 100 years after that. When pellagra became widespread in the southeastern U.S. in the early twentieth century, Dr. Joseph Goldberger proved that the disease was caused by poor nutrition and showed that protein-rich foods like meat and eggs could alleviate its symptoms. Nevertheless, eating these expensive foods was beyond the means of many pellagra sufferers.
Today, maize products in the U.S. are fortified with niacin, which helps to prevent the disease, and pellagra is rare. People worldwide who suffer from pellagra today often face food insecurity for a variety of reasons, like poverty or displacement (for example, refugees).

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
This is documented — Sara Handy McClintock worried that her youngest daughter Barbara was so absorbed in her own interests, so self-contained, so fundamentally uninterested in the social machinery that organized the lives of women in the early twentieth century, that she might not be able to function in the world the way the world required. Sara actually opposed Barbara's enrollment at Cornell, concerned that higher education would make her even less marriageable than she already seemed likely to be.
Barbara McClintock's father, a physician, supported her. He intervened. She enrolled.
She was born Eleanor McClintock on June 16, 1902, in Hartford, Connecticut, the third of four children of Thomas Henry McClintock and Sara Handy McClintock. In 1908, the family moved to Brooklyn, New York, and she grew up there in the specific combination of urban stimulation and domestic expectation that confronted bright girls of her generation — brilliant in school, curious about everything, and being prepared for a future in which her brilliance would be secondary to her availability as a wife. She graduated from Erasmus Hall High School in 1919 and enrolled at Cornell's College of Agriculture.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
Women were not permitted to major in genetics at Cornell. She enrolled in botany and used it as the vehicle for doing what she had actually come to do. She moved into the maize cytogenetics group led by R.A. Emerson, found her people, and began the work that would occupy her entire professional life: looking at the chromosomes of corn under a microscope, developing the staining techniques that made individual chromosomes visible and distinguishable, building the tools that would eventually allow her to see things no one had ever seen before.
She received her BS in 1923, her master's in 1925, her PhD in 1927. She mapped the chromosomes of maize and in 1931, with her colleague Harriet Creighton, published the paper that established chromosomes as the physical basis of genetics — the paper that proved that the abstract entities geneticists had been theorizing about were real, specific, visible physical structures. Thomas Hunt Morgan, who won the Nobel Prize for genetics work in 1933, called the Creighton-McClintock paper the most important paper in genetics that year.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She was elected vice president of the Genetics Society of America in 1939 and president in 1944. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1933, traveled to Germany to study, and left early when she understood what Nazism was going to become. She had produced the first genetic map of maize — a complete diagram of which genes were located where on which chromosome — before anyone had identified the structure of DNA, before the word "genome" was in use, before the molecular biology revolution that would transform everything she was doing.
She was, before 1951, one of the most respected cytogeneticists in the world.
Then she presented what she had actually found.
In 1944, working in her laboratory at the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on Long Island — where she had moved in 1941 for a research position at the Carnegie Institution of Washington — she had begun observing something that the established understanding of genetics said was impossible. She was watching the pigmentation patterns of maize kernels change in ways that shouldn't happen if genes were fixed and immovable. The patterns of color across successive generations of corn ears were too irregular, too responsive, too patterned in their irregularity to be explained by simple mutation.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She traced the patterns backward and forward through generations of plants, correlating the visible pigmentation changes with microscopic examination of the chromosomes. What she found was that certain genetic elements were moving. They were physically relocating from one position on the chromosome to another. They were appearing in new locations and disappearing from old ones. They were turning neighboring genes on and off by their presence and absence.
She called them "controlling elements." She had the data. She had the evidence. She had traced these movements across years of experiments, generation by generation, with the precision of someone who had been reading chromosomes under a microscope for twenty-five years and who trusted what she saw.
In the summer of 1951, at the Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology, she stood before an audience of the leading geneticists of the era and presented her findings.
The field was not ready.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
The molecular biology revolution was just beginning. Watson and Crick were still working on the structure of DNA; they would publish their famous paper in 1953. The scientific community's entire attention was focused on the chemical structure of the gene, on DNA as the molecule of heredity, on the mechanics of how genetic information was stored and transmitted. The idea that genes could move — could regulate each other, could be switched on and off, could function as a dynamic system rather than a static blueprint — was not a question that the field was currently asking, and therefore not a question it was prepared to receive an answer to.
The reaction to her 1951 presentation was, as she described it: "I was startled when I found they didn't understand it. Either I wasn't making it clear, or the framework was not one that they could accept."
She tried again. She presented the work at subsequent symposia. She published in the Carnegie Institution Year Books — the annual reports of the institution that funded her, detailed technical accounts of her findings that were available to specialists but did not circulate through the mainstream of the field. She corresponded with colleagues who were trying to understand what she was describing. She kept planting corn, growing it, harvesting it, examining kernels, examining chromosomes, extending the evidence year by year.
And she largely stopped trying to persuade.

She had said what she had found. She could see that the field didn't have the equipment to receive it yet. She was not the kind of person who revised what she had actually seen in order to be better understood; she was the kind of person who had told the truth, in full, and would wait for the world to catch up. "It might seem unfair to reward a person for having so much pleasure, over the years, asking the maize plant to solve specific problems and then watching its responses," she said at the Nobel ceremony, in characterization of her own work that was partly accurate and partly the understatement of someone who had been ignored for thirty years.
In the 1960s, French biologists Jacques Monod and François Jacob discovered the operon — a genetic regulatory system in bacteria in which genes turned each other on and off through molecular switches. They won the Nobel Prize in 1965. Their work, in the language of molecular biology, demonstrated exactly what McClintock had been describing in maize in the language of classical cytogenetics. The scientific community began to look back at what she had said in 1951.

In the 1970s, molecular biologists, using the new tools of recombinant DNA, began to isolate and characterize transposable elements — jumping genes — in bacteria and in fruit flies. They were everywhere. They were in every organism studied. They were one of the fundamental mechanisms of genetic regulation, genetic evolution, and genetic variation. They were exactly what Barbara McClintock had described in corn, with a microscope, twenty years before molecular biology had the tools to see them.
The Nobel Committee called on October 10, 1983. She was alone in her laboratory. The call was from Stockholm. She had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of mobile genetic elements.
She was eighty-one years old. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine as the sole recipient, unshared with any co-winner.
"It was just a matter of not being able to accept the fact that the chromosomes were dynamic," she said, describing why the field had not understood what she had shown them in 1951. There was no bitterness in the assessment. She was describing a historical reality about the limits of scientific understanding at a particular moment, and she had never taken it personally in the way that it might have been taken personally, because the work had always been between her and the corn plants, and the corn plants had always behaved exactly as she had documented.

She was elected vice president of the Genetics Society of America in 1939 and president in 1944. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1933, traveled to Germany to study, and left early when she understood what Nazism was going to become. She had produced the first genetic map of maize — a complete diagram of which genes were located where on which chromosome — before anyone had identified the structure of DNA, before the word "genome" was in use, before the molecular biology revolution that would transform everything she was doing.
She was, before 1951, one of the most respected cytogeneticists in the world.
Then she presented what she had actually found.
In 1944, working in her laboratory at the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on Long Island — where she had moved in 1941 for a research position at the Carnegie Institution of Washington — she had begun observing something that the established understanding of genetics said was impossible. She was watching the pigmentation patterns of maize kernels change in ways that shouldn't happen if genes were fixed and immovable. The patterns of color across successive generations of corn ears were too irregular, too responsive, too patterned in their irregularity to be explained by simple mutation.

## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She traced the patterns backward and forward through generations of plants, correlating the visible pigmentation changes with microscopic examination of the chromosomes. What she found was that certain genetic elements were moving. They were physically relocating from one position on the chromosome to another. They were appearing in new locations and disappearing from old ones. They were turning neighboring genes on and off by their presence and absence.
She called them "controlling elements." She had the data. She had the evidence. She had traced these movements across years of experiments, generation by generation, with the precision of someone who had been reading chromosomes under a microscope for twenty-five years and who trusted what she saw.
In the summer of 1951, at the Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology, she stood before an audience of the leading geneticists of the era and presented her findings.
The field was not ready.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
The molecular biology revolution was just beginning. Watson and Crick were still working on the structure of DNA; they would publish their famous paper in 1953. The scientific community's entire attention was focused on the chemical structure of the gene, on DNA as the molecule of heredity, on the mechanics of how genetic information was stored and transmitted. The idea that genes could move — could regulate each other, could be switched on and off, could function as a dynamic system rather than a static blueprint — was not a question that the field was currently asking, and therefore not a question it was prepared to receive an answer to.
The reaction to her 1951 presentation was, as she described it: "I was startled when I found they didn't understand it. Either I wasn't making it clear, or the framework was not one that they could accept."
She tried again. She presented the work at subsequent symposia. She published in the Carnegie Institution Year Books — the annual reports of the institution that funded her, detailed technical accounts of her findings that were available to specialists but did not circulate through the mainstream of the field. She corresponded with colleagues who were trying to understand what she was describing. She kept planting corn, growing it, harvesting it, examining kernels, examining chromosomes, extending the evidence year by year.
And she largely stopped trying to persuade.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She had said what she had found. She could see that the field didn't have the equipment to receive it yet. She was not the kind of person who revised what she had actually seen in order to be better understood; she was the kind of person who had told the truth, in full, and would wait for the world to catch up. "It might seem unfair to reward a person for having so much pleasure, over the years, asking the maize plant to solve specific problems and then watching its responses," she said at the Nobel ceremony, in characterization of her own work that was partly accurate and partly the understatement of someone who had been ignored for thirty years.
In the 1960s, French biologists Jacques Monod and François Jacob discovered the operon — a genetic regulatory system in bacteria in which genes turned each other on and off through molecular switches. They won the Nobel Prize in 1965. Their work, in the language of molecular biology, demonstrated exactly what McClintock had been describing in maize in the language of classical cytogenetics. The scientific community began to look back at what she had said in 1951.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
In the 1970s, molecular biologists, using the new tools of recombinant DNA, began to isolate and characterize transposable elements — jumping genes — in bacteria and in fruit flies. They were everywhere. They were in every organism studied. They were one of the fundamental mechanisms of genetic regulation, genetic evolution, and genetic variation. They were exactly what Barbara McClintock had described in corn, with a microscope, twenty years before molecular biology had the tools to see them.
The Nobel Committee called on October 10, 1983. She was alone in her laboratory. The call was from Stockholm. She had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of mobile genetic elements.
She was eighty-one years old. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine as the sole recipient, unshared with any co-winner.
"It was just a matter of not being able to accept the fact that the chromosomes were dynamic," she said, describing why the field had not understood what she had shown them in 1951. There was no bitterness in the assessment. She was describing a historical reality about the limits of scientific understanding at a particular moment, and she had never taken it personally in the way that it might have been taken personally, because the work had always been between her and the corn plants, and the corn plants had always behaved exactly as she had documented.

## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
The molecular biology revolution was just beginning. Watson and Crick were still working on the structure of DNA; they would publish their famous paper in 1953. The scientific community's entire attention was focused on the chemical structure of the gene, on DNA as the molecule of heredity, on the mechanics of how genetic information was stored and transmitted. The idea that genes could move — could regulate each other, could be switched on and off, could function as a dynamic system rather than a static blueprint — was not a question that the field was currently asking, and therefore not a question it was prepared to receive an answer to.
The reaction to her 1951 presentation was, as she described it: "I was startled when I found they didn't understand it. Either I wasn't making it clear, or the framework was not one that they could accept."
She tried again. She presented the work at subsequent symposia. She published in the Carnegie Institution Year Books — the annual reports of the institution that funded her, detailed technical accounts of her findings that were available to specialists but did not circulate through the mainstream of the field. She corresponded with colleagues who were trying to understand what she was describing. She kept planting corn, growing it, harvesting it, examining kernels, examining chromosomes, extending the evidence year by year.
And she largely stopped trying to persuade.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She had said what she had found. She could see that the field didn't have the equipment to receive it yet. She was not the kind of person who revised what she had actually seen in order to be better understood; she was the kind of person who had told the truth, in full, and would wait for the world to catch up. "It might seem unfair to reward a person for having so much pleasure, over the years, asking the maize plant to solve specific problems and then watching its responses," she said at the Nobel ceremony, in characterization of her own work that was partly accurate and partly the understatement of someone who had been ignored for thirty years.
In the 1960s, French biologists Jacques Monod and François Jacob discovered the operon — a genetic regulatory system in bacteria in which genes turned each other on and off through molecular switches. They won the Nobel Prize in 1965. Their work, in the language of molecular biology, demonstrated exactly what McClintock had been describing in maize in the language of classical cytogenetics. The scientific community began to look back at what she had said in 1951.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
In the 1970s, molecular biologists, using the new tools of recombinant DNA, began to isolate and characterize transposable elements — jumping genes — in bacteria and in fruit flies. They were everywhere. They were in every organism studied. They were one of the fundamental mechanisms of genetic regulation, genetic evolution, and genetic variation. They were exactly what Barbara McClintock had described in corn, with a microscope, twenty years before molecular biology had the tools to see them.
The Nobel Committee called on October 10, 1983. She was alone in her laboratory. The call was from Stockholm. She had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of mobile genetic elements.
She was eighty-one years old. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine as the sole recipient, unshared with any co-winner.
"It was just a matter of not being able to accept the fact that the chromosomes were dynamic," she said, describing why the field had not understood what she had shown them in 1951. There was no bitterness in the assessment. She was describing a historical reality about the limits of scientific understanding at a particular moment, and she had never taken it personally in the way that it might have been taken personally, because the work had always been between her and the corn plants, and the corn plants had always behaved exactly as she had documented.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She died on September 2, 1992, at Huntington, New York. She was ninety years old. She had spent over sixty years examining the chromosomes of maize and had been right about all of it before the field had the language to understand what she was saying.
Her mother had worried she was too independent.
She was. That was the whole point.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
This is documented — Sara Handy McClintock worried that her youngest daughter Barbara was so absorbed in her own interests, so self-contained, so fundamentally uninterested in the social machinery that organized the lives of women in the early twentieth century, that she might not be able to function in the world the way the world required. Sara actually opposed Barbara's enrollment at Cornell, concerned that higher education would make her even less marriageable than she already seemed likely to be.
Barbara McClintock's father, a physician, supported her. He intervened. She enrolled.
She was born Eleanor McClintock on June 16, 1902, in Hartford, Connecticut, the third of four children of Thomas Henry McClintock and Sara Handy McClintock. In 1908, the family moved to Brooklyn, New York, and she grew up there in the specific combination of urban stimulation and domestic expectation that confronted bright girls of her generation — brilliant in school, curious about everything, and being prepared for a future in which her brilliance would be secondary to her availability as a wife. She graduated from Erasmus Hall High School in 1919 and enrolled at Cornell's College of Agriculture.

Women were not permitted to major in genetics at Cornell. She enrolled in botany and used it as the vehicle for doing what she had actually come to do. She moved into the maize cytogenetics group led by R.A. Emerson, found her people, and began the work that would occupy her entire professional life: looking at the chromosomes of corn under a microscope, developing the staining techniques that made individual chromosomes visible and distinguishable, building the tools that would eventually allow her to see things no one had ever seen before.
She received her BS in 1923, her master's in 1925, her PhD in 1927. She mapped the chromosomes of maize and in 1931, with her colleague Harriet Creighton, published the paper that established chromosomes as the physical basis of genetics — the paper that proved that the abstract entities geneticists had been theorizing about were real, specific, visible physical structures. Thomas Hunt Morgan, who won the Nobel Prize for genetics work in 1933, called the Creighton-McClintock paper the most important paper in genetics that year.

She was elected vice president of the Genetics Society of America in 1939 and president in 1944. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1933, traveled to Germany to study, and left early when she understood what Nazism was going to become. She had produced the first genetic map of maize — a complete diagram of which genes were located where on which chromosome — before anyone had identified the structure of DNA, before the word "genome" was in use, before the molecular biology revolution that would transform everything she was doing.
She was, before 1951, one of the most respected cytogeneticists in the world.
Then she presented what she had actually found.
In 1944, working in her laboratory at the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on Long Island — where she had moved in 1941 for a research position at the Carnegie Institution of Washington — she had begun observing something that the established understanding of genetics said was impossible. She was watching the pigmentation patterns of maize kernels change in ways that shouldn't happen if genes were fixed and immovable. The patterns of color across successive generations of corn ears were too irregular, too responsive, too patterned in their irregularity to be explained by simple mutation.

## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She traced the patterns backward and forward through generations of plants, correlating the visible pigmentation changes with microscopic examination of the chromosomes. What she found was that certain genetic elements were moving. They were physically relocating from one position on the chromosome to another. They were appearing in new locations and disappearing from old ones. They were turning neighboring genes on and off by their presence and absence.
She called them "controlling elements." She had the data. She had the evidence. She had traced these movements across years of experiments, generation by generation, with the precision of someone who had been reading chromosomes under a microscope for twenty-five years and who trusted what she saw.
In the summer of 1951, at the Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology, she stood before an audience of the leading geneticists of the era and presented her findings.
The field was not ready.

# Fact That Will Blow Your Mind | Her mother thought she was too independent | Facebook
## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
The molecular biology revolution was just beginning. Watson and Crick were still working on the structure of DNA; they would publish their famous paper in 1953. The scientific community's entire attention was focused on the chemical structure of the gene, on DNA as the molecule of heredity, on the mechanics of how genetic information was stored and transmitted. The idea that genes could move — could regulate each other, could be switched on and off, could function as a dynamic system rather than a static blueprint — was not a question that the field was currently asking, and therefore not a question it was prepared to receive an answer to.
The reaction to her 1951 presentation was, as she described it: "I was startled when I found they didn't understand it. Either I wasn't making it clear, or the framework was not one that they could accept."
She tried again. She presented the work at subsequent symposia. She published in the Carnegie Institution Year Books — the annual reports of the institution that funded her, detailed technical accounts of her findings that were available to specialists but did not circulate through the mainstream of the field. She corresponded with colleagues who were trying to understand what she was describing. She kept planting corn, growing it, harvesting it, examining kernels, examining chromosomes, extending the evidence year by year.
And she largely stopped trying to persuade.

## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
She had said what she had found. She could see that the field didn't have the equipment to receive it yet. She was not the kind of person who revised what she had actually seen in order to be better understood; she was the kind of person who had told the truth, in full, and would wait for the world to catch up. "It might seem unfair to reward a person for having so much pleasure, over the years, asking the maize plant to solve specific problems and then watching its responses," she said at the Nobel ceremony, in characterization of her own work that was partly accurate and partly the understatement of someone who had been ignored for thirty years.
In the 1960s, French biologists Jacques Monod and François Jacob discovered the operon — a genetic regulatory system in bacteria in which genes turned each other on and off through molecular switches. They won the Nobel Prize in 1965. Their work, in the language of molecular biology, demonstrated exactly what McClintock had been describing in maize in the language of classical cytogenetics. The scientific community began to look back at what she had said in 1951.

## [Fact That Will Blow Your Mind](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1448602192711619/?__cft__[0]=AZgRQHhMtnGbOCs6i2IOU6MWmFLeLvRlKT5GVzz7ZVhpmEEgjsVjRfjTa4lwwMmErnf9Y_VwhhVk4dSHUbhrM_5VwLeiq41khrhAXLK1husWO33iMVlgQnkl25rwBY4q4bDFOYLhAiLXPbmFT_Qxu5syBcTR5LoYkxUM47-WjyguUcjTiQ6wWMORGwqK_pZVAxXM&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
In the 1970s, molecular biologists, using the new tools of recombinant DNA, began to isolate and characterize transposable elements — jumping genes — in bacteria and in fruit flies. They were everywhere. They were in every organism studied. They were one of the fundamental mechanisms of genetic regulation, genetic evolution, and genetic variation. They were exactly what Barbara McClintock had described in corn, with a microscope, twenty years before molecular biology had the tools to see them.
The Nobel Committee called on October 10, 1983. She was alone in her laboratory. The call was from Stockholm. She had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of mobile genetic elements.
She was eighty-one years old. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine as the sole recipient, unshared with any co-winner.
"It was just a matter of not being able to accept the fact that the chromosomes were dynamic," she said, describing why the field had not understood what she had shown them in 1951. There was no bitterness in the assessment. She was describing a historical reality about the limits of scientific understanding at a particular moment, and she had never taken it personally in the way that it might have been taken personally, because the work had always been between her and the corn plants, and the corn plants had always behaved exactly as she had documented.
